t.1.164.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Having then heard those words of the Gandharva, O bull of the Bharatas, Arjuna shone with supreme delight like the full moon.
t.1.164.2: And the great archer, best of the Kurus, his curiosity greatly aroused by the power of Vasiṣṭha's austerities, spoke to the Gandharva.
t.1.164.3: The seer whose name you have uttered as Vasiṣṭha, about him I wish to hear; tell me of it exactly as it was.
t.1.164.4: O lord of the Gandharvas, tell me this: who is this blessed seer who was the purohita of our forefathers?
t.1.164.7: He who, though tormented by the calamity of his sons and powerful and masterful as he was, did not resolve upon a terrible deed for the destruction of Viśvāmitra.
t.1.164.8: Though he was able to bring his dead sons back again from the abode of Yama, he did not overstep the decree of death, just as the great ocean does not overstep its shore.
t.1.164.9: Having obtained him, the self-controlled and great-souled one, the Ikṣvāku kings, lords of men and protectors of the earth, won this whole earth.
t.1.164.10: Having obtained Vasiṣṭha, the best of seers, as their excellent family priest, those kings also performed sacrifices, O joy of the Kurus.
t.1.164.11: For that brahmarṣi, O best of the Pāṇḍavas, officiated at the sacrifices of all those most excellent kings, just as Bṛhaspati did for the immortals.
t.1.164.12: Therefore let some virtuous brahmin be sought out as your family priest, one whose very self is devoted to dharma, who knows the Veda and dharma, and who is agreeable to you.
t.1.164.13: For a kṣatriya who is born and wishes to conquer the earth must first appoint a purohita, O Pārtha, for the increase of his kingdom.
t.1.164.14: A king who seeks to conquer the earth must place a brahmin at his forefront. Therefore let some virtuous twice-born be your family priest.
t.1.164.6: He of noble mind who, though harboring the utmost wrath because of the offense of Viśvāmitra, did not bring about the destruction of the Kuśikas.
t.1.164.5: He whose feet were massaged by Desire and Anger both, which, though unconquerable even by the immortals, had been conquered for ever by his austerity.
